extracted.intended_audience: reporters, rewrite men, and journalism students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing follow-up stories, rewrites, and feature (human-interest and informational) newspaper pieces; covers leads, angles, sources, timeliness, length, style, and ethical restraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: New Facts Featured
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally in the 'follow-up' it is the newly learned facts that are featured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In a sudden death follow-up feature the funeral arrangements; in a railway wreck follow-up present the investigation and the placing of blame. Use newly uncovered details as the lead focus (examples shown: arrest follow-up, recovered body, investigation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Results Featured
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequently the lead to the follow-up features the results effected by the details of the earlier story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lead with the consequences of earlier events (example: government crop report leading to turbulent wheat market prices). Show how earlier details produced current results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probable Results
rubrics_metrics.description: Where no more important details can be learned, it sometimes is wise to feature probable results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When fresh facts are scarce, present likely outcomes or consequences (example: diplomats expecting a break in relations after torpedoing). Use plausible inference to keep story current.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clues for Identification
rubrics_metrics.description: In stories of crime, when the offenders have escaped, the lead to the follow-up may begin with clues for establishing the identity of the criminals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open with identifying descriptions or tips that will help capture or identify suspects (example: physical description of a piano tuner and companion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Featuring Lack of News
rubrics_metrics.description: In rare cases the very fact that there is no additional news is worth featuring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the absence of developments itself the lead (example: nothing heard about a missing prosecuting attorney).

rubrics_metrics.name: Opinions of Prominent Persons
rubrics_metrics.description: An otherwise unimportant follow story may sometimes be made a good one by interviewing prominent persons and localizing the reader's interest in men or women he knows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use authoritative or well-known voices to add significance to a follow-up (example: Health Commissioner Shannon's view on a new law). Localize the issue by quoting local figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary of Opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes, indeed, it is well to interview a number of local persons and make the lead a summary of their views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aggregate varied local reactions into a concise lead that captures community sentiment (example: differing opinions of physicians and clergymen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Connecting Links
rubrics_metrics.description: Sufficient explanatory matter has been included to connect the incidents readily with the events of the preceding days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always provide immediate context so readers who missed earlier stories can relate new events to prior occurrences; include connecting links in or immediately after the lead to give the reader necessary bearings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewrites Must Differ and Seek New Angles
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the duty of the rewrite man to handle such a story, and to handle it in such a way that it shall bear no resemblance to the story published by the other paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Find new features, new angles of view, or new relations between details. Do not simply paraphrase; seek fresh emphasis or connections while remaining truthful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bring Old News Up to the Minute (Currency)
rubrics_metrics.description: The first requisite in rewriting is the necessity of making old news new, of bringing it up to the minute. Currency is all but a necessity to life, vigor, interest in a yesterday's event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present older events so they seem current; avoid beginning with 'yesterday' and instead reposition timing into the paper's present (examples of rewritten leads are provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Using 'Yesterday' in Leads
rubrics_metrics.description: It is also against journalistic rules to begin with 'Dr. Smith was arrested yesterday.' That yesterday must be eliminated from the lead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use present-tense framing or time-relative phrasing that ties the event to the paper's publication moment rather than a dated adverb.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek New Features in Rewrites
rubrics_metrics.description: The next thing to seek in the story to be rewritten is a new feature. Generally this is obtained in bringing the story up to date. If not, the reporter may examine whether the first story plays up the best feature, or whether it does not contain another feature equally good, or one possibly entirely overlooked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no new facts are available, look for causes, motives, related events, probable developments, or patterns (e.g., relation to similar fires or burglaries). Use imagination but 'take care always to make his rewrite truthful.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Condensation in Rewrites
rubrics_metrics.description: Though rewrites are made to seem fresh and new, they are nevertheless old news after all, and hence are not worth so much space as the original; consequently, they usually run from half to a fourth the length of the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cut generously ('cut every story to the bone') but do not merely omit paragraphs (excision is not rewriting). Preserve coherence while strongly condensing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature Story: Human-Interest Requires Literary 'Rouge' and a Single Emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: The feature, or human interest, story... its news is a little less excellent and must be made good by the writer's ingenuity. This rouge generally is an adroit appeal to the emotions... by centering the interest in a single emotion and drawing the attention away from lack of piquancy in the details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose and unify around one emotion (love, fear, hate, regret, curiosity, humor, etc.) to make less sensational news attractive; use literary touches judiciously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restraint to Avoid Overemphasis in Features
rubrics_metrics.description: The difficulty lies chiefly in the temptation to overemphasize... In striving to make the story humorous, one goes too far... or in attempting to be pathetic, one is liable to induce mere derisive laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise restraint; a single misplaced word or discordant phrase can destroy the effect. Only skilled writers should attempt heavy emotional or stylistic treatments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two Types of Feature Stories (Human-Interest and Informational)
rubrics_metrics.description: These remarks... apply more specifically to the human interest type, the type the purpose of which is largely to entertain. Certainly it is more difficult than the second, whose purpose is to instruct or inform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Human-interest features derive appeal from emotion; informational features attract by curiosity and instruction (examples given). Choose style and approach according to type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness for Informational Features
rubrics_metrics.description: Timeliness is not essential, but is valuable, as in the publication of Halloween, Christmas, Easter, and vacation stories at their appropriate seasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schedule and angle informational features to seasonal or topical relevance when possible to increase reader interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources and Requirement of Personal Observation
rubrics_metrics.description: The sources of feature stories are everywhere... The only requirement in obtaining information is personal observation and investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draw from street observation, clubs, courts, athletic fields, journals, government publications, old residents, travelers, etc. Use original reporting and local witnesses; photographs enhance value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and Use of Informal Leads
rubrics_metrics.description: The form of the feature story is anomalous. It has none. One is at liberty to begin in any way likely to attract the reader... informal leads are the rule rather than the exception — leads that will arrest attention by telling enough of the story to excite curiosity without giving all the details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open with a vivid, suspensive or teasing lead that provokes curiosity (multiple lead examples provided). Do not be bound to inverted-pyramid norms for features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspense and Unique Style as Devices
rubrics_metrics.description: In some feature stories the writers attempt to hold their readers' interest by making the narrative suspensive throughout... a writer will resort to uniqueness of form or style to get his effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sustain suspense or adopt a unique stylistic approach when fitting, but balance novelty with clarity and restraint. Examples show sustained suspense leads and quirky forms.
